item.title: Three Hours, One Ultimatum: Trump's Unannounced Iran Talks After His "Annihilate" Warning at the UN
item.body:
On the same day President Donald Trump told the United Nations General Assembly that Iran faces a stark choice, his envoys sat down for roughly three hours of talks with an Iranian delegation on the sidelines of the summit. The meeting had not been announced beforehand. It came to light when Trump described it to reporters.

The pairing of a blunt public threat with quiet diplomacy shows how U.S.–Iran relations are being handled at a tense moment, nearly seven months into a conflict that has reshaped energy markets and Middle East politics. Here is what is known so far, based on public reporting, and what remains unclear.

## The Warning at the UN

In his address to world leaders, Trump framed the situation as a binary choice. According to reports of the speech, he asked whether he should "annihilate the Islamic Republic" and do so quickly, or whether a negotiated agreement could still be reached. Speaking to reporters afterward, he described the alternatives as "obliteration" on one side and "potential greatness" for Iran on the other.

The language was among the most forceful Trump has used toward Tehran at a multilateral forum. It was also a negotiating position: an ultimatum meant to signal that the window for a deal is limited, and that the alternative is severe.

## The Three-Hour Meeting

Shortly after the speech, Trump said U.S. and Iranian officials had met at the UN General Assembly, and he called the session "very good" and "very productive." Participants named in reports include:

- **Steve Witkoff**, Trump's special envoy
- **Jared Kushner**, Trump's son-in-law and informal adviser
- **Abbas Araghchi**, Iran's foreign minister

Coverage differs on the format. Some accounts describe a face-to-face meeting. At least one report said mediators shuttled between the two sides. The White House and Tehran may give further detail in the coming days. Trump also said another round of talks would take place in the very near future, though no date has been publicly confirmed.

## What Iran Says It Wants

Iranian state broadcaster IRIB said Araghchi laid out Tehran's conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway that carries a large share of the world's seaborne oil. According to that account, Iran is asking for:

- An immediate end to the U.S. naval blockade
- Release of frozen Iranian assets
- An end to the fighting on all fronts, including Lebanon

Washington's stated priorities point in a different direction. Reporting on the talks says the U.S. wants free navigation through the strait and firm limits on Iran's nuclear program. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the administration remained open to further engagement if it could lead to real progress, and he repeated the core U.S. goal that Iran never obtain a nuclear weapon.

## Hard Words on Both Sides

Iran's response to the "annihilate" remark was also defiant. Iran's General Staff said its forces were ready to carry out strikes that would be "more crushing and less predictable" than earlier attacks, according to Al Jazeera.

Analysts caution against reading the rhetoric as a sign that talks are failing. Andreas Krieg of King's College London told Al Jazeera that the escalating language works as a "bargaining strategy," letting each government project strength at home while keeping room to negotiate. On that reading, tough public statements and private meetings are two parts of one process rather than a contradiction.

## The Midterm Factor

Timing is a central question. Trump indicated that a final agreement may not arrive before the November midterm elections, although accounts of his remarks on the timeline have varied slightly, so it is worth watching for clarification.

Domestic politics may be shaping the calendar. The conflict has pushed up U.S. fuel prices, according to Al Jazeera, and energy costs are a sensitive issue for voters. A deal that reopens the Strait of Hormuz could ease that pressure. A deal seen as too generous could draw criticism from opponents in Washington and from U.S. allies in the region. That tension helps explain why both outcomes, a breakthrough and a delay, remain plausible.

## What to Watch Next

- **A second round of talks.** Trump said one is coming soon. Whether it is confirmed, and at what level, will signal how serious the process is.
- **The Strait of Hormuz and the blockade.** Any easing of either would be the clearest sign of progress.
- **Nuclear terms.** Public detail on enrichment limits and inspections has been scarce.
- **Rhetoric versus action.** Watch whether military statements from either side are followed by real escalation or fade as talks continue.

## The Bottom Line

The UN meeting did not produce a deal, and neither side has said it did. It did show that direct or mediated communication between Washington and Tehran is active even as both governments trade sharp warnings in public. Whether that channel leads to an agreement, or whether the ultimatum hardens positions, is likely to become clearer in the weeks before the midterms.

*This article summarizes publicly available reporting as of September 24, 2026. Details of the talks are based on statements from officials and news organizations and may change as the situation develops.*

**Sources:** [The Times of Israel](https://www.timesofisrael.com/us-and-iranian-negotiators-hold-talks-at-un-that-trump-says-went-very-well/), [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/23/annihilate-vs-crushing-attacks-why-iran-us-up-rhetoric-amid-talks), [Axios](https://www.axios.com/2026/09/22/unga-iran-us-trump-war), [The Week](https://www.theweek.in/news/middle-east/2026/09/23/us-iran-meeting-unga-trump-annihilation-threat.html)
